title: 5 Best Qualtrics Text iQ Alternatives for Insights Teams
summary: Qualtrics Text iQ alternatives for teams staying on Qualtrics for collection. Five options, what Text iQ actually limits, and how Text iQ differs from XM Discover.
body_markdown:
You already own Qualtrics. Surveys go out, responses come back, and the open-ended box at the end of each one is where the useful material lives. Text iQ is what Qualtrics gives you to read it, and for a while it works. Then the topic list gets long, the tagging goes stale, someone asks which theme moved net promoter score (NPS), and you're back in a spreadsheet.


What most Qualtrics customers want here isn't a replacement survey platform. It's a replacement analysis layer. Thematic is built for that position: you keep Qualtrics for collection, and Thematic takes the verbatims and builds the theme structure, the impact analysis, and the reporting on top. Thematic is not survey-only either: add another feedback channel later and the same taxonomy extends to it rather than being rebuilt. Thematic has a[1-click integration with Qualtrics](https://getthematic.com/integrations/qualtrics) , so the survey program you already run doesn't change. That strength carries a matching cost. Thematic doesn't distribute surveys. It's an analytics layer, not a collection tool.


Below is the list, plus one section that matters more than it sounds. Text iQ and Qualtrics XM Discover are not the same product, and pages on this query blur them.


## Text iQ is not XM Discover. Check which one you have.


Qualtrics sells two things that both do text analytics. The buying decision changes completely depending on which one you've hit the ceiling of.


- **Qualtrics Text iQ** is included functionality inside the core survey platform, living in the Data and Analysis tab of a survey or employee experience project.[Qualtrics describes topics in Text iQ](https://www.qualtrics.com/support/survey-platform/data-and-analysis-module/text-iq/topics-in-text-iq/) as "a great way of tagging your text responses." You create them by clicking a plus sign on a response, by writing search queries, or by importing from the Qualtrics topic library. Whoever owns the survey owns Text iQ.
- **Qualtrics XM Discover** is the former Clarabridge Studio product, sold separately, with its own documentation tree.[Qualtrics says](https://www.qualtrics.com/support/xm-discover/getting-started-discover/xm-discover-basic-overview/) it "consists of 3 applications: Connectors, Designer and Studio," and that it analyzes feedback "including cases, chat, voice transcriptions, emails, surveys, ratings, and reviews on third party websites, social media, and online communities." Contact center teams buy it.


Qualtrics keeps them apart itself. Its newer[Text Analytics documentation](https://www.qualtrics.com/support/omnichannel-listening/text-analytics-xm/text-analytics-overview/) says you can use unstructured text "from the Qualtrics platform or XM Discover," then states: "Text Analytics is not compatible with Text iQ. The same text data cannot be used in both a topic model and within Text iQ in a survey."


If what's frustrating you is an omnichannel contact center deployment rather than a survey tab, read the[XM Discover alternatives list](https://getthematic.com/insights/best-xm-discover-alternatives) instead. Everything below assumes Text iQ.


## What actually breaks in Text iQ


Five limits show up repeatedly. Qualtrics documents three of them itself.


- **The taxonomy is per question, not per program.** Text iQ topics live inside an individual question, so a tracker with forty open-ended questions means forty separate topic sets to build and maintain. Nothing you define for one question carries to the next, and the work repeats every time the questionnaire changes.
- **Topics are something you build and maintain.** The default path is manual tagging or search-query rules you write. On[Thematic's own published benchmarks](https://getthematic.com/insights/ai-feedback-analytics-accuracy) , rule-based approaches run at roughly 60 to 70 percent accuracy, against 80 to 90 percent for themes built from the data itself.
- **There's a hard ceiling on topic count.** Qualtrics states that "each question in Text iQ has a limit of 350 parent topics and 350 topics, total." Generous for one question. For a long-running program with a mature code frame, it's a wall you can see coming.
- **The good parts are license-gated.**[Qualtrics states](https://www.qualtrics.com/support/survey-platform/data-and-analysis-module/text-iq/sentiment-analysis/) that "Sentiment Analysis is only available to Advanced Text clients," and recommended topics are Advanced-only too. Standard-license teams do more by hand than they expected.
- **Scope stops at the survey.** Text iQ sees the data that arrived through a Qualtrics survey. App reviews, call transcripts and other channels are somewhere else. Qualtrics' newer Text Analytics layer can combine projects, but Qualtrics states that "Text Analytics is not compatible with Text iQ. The same text data cannot be used in both a topic model and within Text iQ in a survey," so moving to it is a migration rather than an addition.


## The list at a glance


1. **Thematic.** Analytics layer that sits on top of Qualtrics and builds an inspectable theme taxonomy tied to score impact.
2. **Qualtrics XM Discover.** The omnichannel upgrade inside the Qualtrics estate, for teams whose real problem is contact-center voice.
3. **Chattermill.** Broad channel consolidation for CX teams who need one view across many feedback sources.
4. **Enterpret.** Product-org oriented taxonomy tooling, strongest when the consumer of the insight is engineering.
5. **Relative Insight.** Comparative language analysis for researchers asking how two groups talk differently.


## 1. Thematic


**Thematic is the option for a Qualtrics customer who wants to keep the survey program and change only what happens to the verbatims.** Point it at your open-ended responses and the theme structure comes out of the answers themselves, two levels deep, with no rules or keyword dictionaries to maintain. Add a second survey or another channel later and the themes you already have carry across instead of the structure being rebuilt.


Two things matter for a researcher specifically. First, the taxonomy stays inspectable. A researcher can trace any theme back to the verbatims that created it, adjust what belongs in it, and stand behind the number in a readout. Second, the Themes Editor runs 18 evaluation checks across your hierarchy and untagged comments, returning a prioritized list: themes that should merge, subthemes under the wrong parent, themes too generic to act on, comment clusters warranting a new theme. Thematic publishes the caveat alongside it. "The AI doesn't have your business context, so a suggestion that looks reasonable may not fit your analytical goals."


Theme upkeep runs as a Theme Maintenance workflow, configured per lens, on a monthly schedule. Coverage maintenance "expands the phrases mapped to your existing themes so new feedback keeps matching." New themes are surfaced "for you to review and approve" rather than applied, because a new theme changes the shape of every analysis already built on it.


**What it looks like in practice.** Smith and Smith, New Zealand's leading vehicle glass repair business and part of the Belron group, built its stack in exactly this shape: Qualtrics to gather feedback across all company locations and all customer journey points, Thematic to discover themes and tie them to[the impact on NPS scores](https://getthematic.com/insights/link-feedback-themes-nps-csat-drivers) , Power BI to distribute the result. Carlos Reyes, Senior Insights Analyst, was the analyst behind it. Thematic's writeup puts the reason plainly: "Both Power BI and Qualtrics have some text analysis capabilities, but they aren't advanced enough to easily answer the questions insights teams get from their stakeholders."


**Choose something else instead of Thematic if:** you need the tool to collect the feedback as well as analyze it. Thematic doesn't distribute surveys and doesn't replace Qualtrics. If your goal is consolidating to one vendor, an analytics layer adds one rather than removing one.


## 2. Qualtrics XM Discover


**XM Discover is the upgrade for a team whose real problem turned out to be contact-center voice, not analysis quality.** It reaches the contact center calls, chat and review sites Text iQ never sees, through three applications Qualtrics names as Connectors, Designer and Studio. It's a separate purchase with its own implementation and learning curve. A survey owner who wanted better themes in one study will find it larger than the problem.


**Choose it instead of Thematic if:** you have contact center voice and chat volume that has to be analyzed in the same place as your survey data, and you want a single vendor accountable for all of it.


## 3. Chattermill


**Chattermill is aimed at CX teams consolidating many feedback sources into one view.** It calls itself an AI-native CX intelligence and Voice of Customer platform that "connects with 65+ feedback channels," and says feedback is "analyzed across 100+ languages, with automated translation and transcription built in." For a Qualtrics-centric research team, that breadth is the thing to press on. If most of your volume is survey verbatims, you're buying coverage you won't use in year one.


**Choose it instead of Thematic if:** language coverage is a hard requirement, or your feedback really is spread across dozens of sources and cutting the number of tools people log into matters more than theme depth.


## 4. Enterpret


**Enterpret is oriented toward product organizations rather than research teams.** It positions itself as "customer intelligence infrastructure" for "product, customer experience, support, operations, and GTM teams at high-velocity product organizations," built around an Adaptive Taxonomy that structures signals into shared themes and categories. The framing tells you who it's for. The value lands when the consumer of the insight is a product manager deciding what to build next, not an analyst defending a method.


**Choose it instead of Thematic if:** your primary stakeholder is a product org, your feedback is dominated by tickets and reviews rather than survey verbatims, and you want themes flowing into engineering tools.


## 5. Relative Insight


**Relative Insight is the outlier on this list, and the most interesting one for a researcher.** Its method is comparative language analysis. Instead of asking what themes exist, it asks how the language of one group differs from another. Detractors against promoters. This quarter against last. It leans on traceability, stating that "every answer is grounded only in your own data, verified and traceable back to source" and that "every result is reproducible and auditable." For a research function that has to show its working, that's aimed at you.


**Choose it instead of Thematic if:** your recurring question is a comparison between two defined groups rather than ongoing measurement of a theme set over time.


## How to choose between them


Five questions that separate these faster than a feature matrix.


1. **Which Qualtrics product am I actually on?** Check whether your text analytics lives in the Data and Analysis tab of a survey, or in a separate application suite. If it's the second, this is the wrong list.
2. **Am I replacing collection, or only analysis?** If Qualtrics stays, you're shopping for a layer and should test the integration path first. If it doesn't, you want the[wider Qualtrics shortlist](https://getthematic.com/insights/best-qualtrics-alternatives-feedback-analytics) .
3. **How much of my feedback is survey verbatims?** If almost all of it is, channel breadth is capability you'll pay for and not use. If most of it isn't, it's the whole point.
4. **Who has to be convinced by the output?** If a stakeholder will challenge a theme, you need to open it, see how it was built, and change it. Ask every vendor to show that screen, not a dashboard.
5. **What happens to the taxonomy in month nine?** Ask what maintains it, on what schedule, and whether new themes appear without anyone approving them. A model that changes your categories quietly breaks every trend line you've drawn.


One note on budget. None of these vendors publish pricing on their own sites, Qualtrics included. Any number on a comparison site is an estimate, so treat it as one.


## The short version


For most Qualtrics customers hitting the ceiling of Text iQ, the strongest move is to keep Qualtrics for collection and add Thematic as the analysis layer on top. That's the architecture Smith and Smith built, with Power BI on the end of it. Thematic doesn't distribute surveys, so this adds a vendor rather than consolidating one. If your real problem is channel coverage rather than theme quality, Qualtrics XM Discover is the better answer, and staying inside the estate you already bought isn't a failure. Either way, confirm which Qualtrics product you're on before the first demo.
